Family Health

Adnexal masses: symptoms, assessment and treatment

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An adnexal mass is a lump or abnormal structure in the region beside the uterus, including the ovaries, fallopian tubes and nearby tissues. It may contain fluid, solid tissue or both. Many causes are benign, but the term describes a finding rather than a final diagnosis. Its appearance, symptoms, pregnancy status and stage of life guide what happens next.

Symptoms and incidental findings

A mass may cause no symptoms and be discovered on a scan or examination for another reason. Possible symptoms include pelvic discomfort, period changes, pain during sex, abdominal swelling, constipation, digestive discomfort, frequent urination or difficulty emptying the bladder. Symptoms depend on the cause as well as size, and none identifies the diagnosis by itself.

Arrange assessment for persistent or worsening symptoms, new unexplained vaginal bleeding, or repeated bloating, early fullness or urinary changes. Tiredness, indigestion, back pain and bowel changes can have many explanations, including occasionally ovarian cancer. Bleeding within a cyst can cause pain, but internal bleeding cannot be diagnosed by looking for visible vaginal blood.

When to seek urgent or emergency care

Sudden severe pelvic or lower abdominal pain, especially with vomiting, needs immediate emergency assessment because ovarian twisting, cyst rupture or bleeding may be responsible. Fainting, marked dizziness, pallor, collapse or severe pain with possible pregnancy can indicate internal bleeding; seek emergency help immediately. Complete inability to pass urine also needs immediate care.

If pregnancy is possible and you have pelvic pain, unusual bleeding or shoulder-tip pain, seek urgent medical advice even without a positive home test. Fever with pelvic pain or rapidly worsening swelling also needs urgent assessment. Do not wait for a planned scan or repeat test when these warning signs occur.

Common benign causes

Functional ovarian cysts arise with the menstrual cycle and often settle over a few weeks or months. Other causes include endometriomas associated with endometriosis, dermoid cysts and cystadenomas. Some benign tumours contain solid tissue; a solid area does not automatically mean cancer, and a fluid-filled structure is not automatically harmless.

A presumed ovarian mass may instead come from a fallopian tube or another nearby structure. Benign tumours do not invade or spread like cancer, but a persistent or large benign lesion can still cause pain, pressure or twisting. The statement that most masses simply disappear applies best to selected functional cysts, not every adnexal finding.

Cancer is a possibility, not a conclusion

Malignant ovarian or nearby tissue growth can enlarge and spread, but many adnexal masses are not cancer. Risk is assessed from imaging features, age and menopause, symptoms, personal and family history and selected tests. Solid components or complex features warrant careful evaluation rather than a diagnosis from one word in a report.

Cancer-related symptoms overlap with common benign conditions. Persistent bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary urgency or unexplained bleeding should be checked rather than dismissed. Suspicious findings may require referral to a gynaecological cancer specialist; a referral does not itself confirm cancer, and outcome cannot be promised before the diagnosis and stage are known.

Ectopic pregnancy is a different urgent cause

An ectopic pregnancy implants outside the uterine cavity, usually in a fallopian tube, and may appear as an adnexal finding. It cannot continue as a normal pregnancy and can rupture, causing life-threatening internal bleeding. Pain or bleeding with possible pregnancy needs prompt assessment; sudden severe pain with faintness or collapse is an emergency.

A pregnancy test is important, but a single test alone does not establish where a pregnancy is located. Clinicians may use transvaginal ultrasound and serial blood hCG measurements, and occasionally surgery. Carefully monitored observation, medication or surgery are selected according to the findings; this is not a condition to watch at home without a clinical plan.

How an adnexal mass is assessed

Assessment includes symptoms, menstrual and pregnancy history, menopause, medicines and relevant family history. An abdominal or pelvic examination may help, but ultrasound is usually the first imaging test. Transvaginal and/or abdominal scanning describes the location, size and internal features; an examination alone cannot reliably identify every mass or exclude cancer.

Selected blood tests, including pregnancy testing and sometimes CA125, can support assessment. CA125 is not a stand-alone cancer diagnosis: benign conditions and pregnancy can alter it, and results must be interpreted in context. Specialist ultrasound or MRI may clarify an indeterminate finding. Imaging risk systems support clinical judgment; routine surveillance schedules do not override acute warning symptoms.

Monitoring, surgery and tissue diagnosis

A small, simple, reassuring cyst without troublesome symptoms may need observation, sometimes with a repeat scan and sometimes without routine follow-up. The clinician should explain the timing and what changes need earlier review. Persistent, growing, complex or symptomatic masses may require further investigation or surgery; a solid component alone does not make an operation inevitable.

Surgical choice depends on the likely cause, cancer concern, complications and fertility goals. Where appropriate, the cyst can be removed while preserving the ovary, but some situations require more extensive surgery. Removed tissue is examined in a laboratory; a malignant result may require further specialist treatment. Neither surgery nor a reassuring scan guarantees that every future symptom can be ignored.

Adnexal masses during pregnancy

Pregnancy scans sometimes find an ovarian cyst or other adnexal mass. Many reassuring cysts can be monitored, and some resolve as pregnancy progresses; persistent, large or complex findings need an individualized follow-up plan. Pregnancy changes how imaging and blood markers are interpreted, and MRI may help when ultrasound is insufficient. Not every mass must be removed before pregnancy or during it.

Severe symptoms, twisting, bleeding or concern for malignancy may justify intervention. Timing balances maternal health, the suspected diagnosis and pregnancy stage with specialist input; urgent problems must not wait simply to prolong pregnancy. A fixed claim that 10% of all pregnancy adnexal masses are malignant is not a reliable personal estimate, and early cancer or a good outcome cannot be assumed.

Outlook and useful follow-up questions

The outlook depends on the actual diagnosis. Functional cysts often resolve, other benign lesions may persist, and cancer requires disease-specific care. Most cysts do not prevent pregnancy, but the underlying condition and any proposed surgery can affect fertility. Discuss ovarian preservation and future pregnancy plans before a non-emergency procedure whenever possible.

Ask where the mass arises, whether it looks simple or complex, whether further tests are needed, when to repeat imaging and what symptoms require earlier help. Keep your follow-up even if symptoms improve unless the clinician changes the plan. A new or worsening symptom deserves reassessment rather than assuming an old benign label explains it.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Distinguish a descriptive adnexal finding from its final diagnosis and cancer risk.

Apply cyst-specific monitoring only when the scan and clinical context are reassuring.

Consider pregnancy location and acute complications before routine surveillance advice.

Discuss fertility goals, individual follow-up and specialist referral when appropriate.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record symptoms, bleeding, test and appointment dates, and questions for your clinician. It cannot diagnose the mass, interpret imaging or CA125, exclude cancer or ectopic pregnancy, or replace a follow-up plan. Do not delay urgent care to complete tracking or wait for an app prediction.

When to seek help

Seek emergency care for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with vomiting, faintness, pallor or collapse, and for complete inability to pass urine. Possible pregnancy with pain, bleeding or shoulder-tip pain needs urgent advice even without a positive home test. Fever, worsening symptoms or persistent unexplained bleeding also require medical review. This guide does not replace individualized assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An adnexal mass describes a location and finding, not a diagnosis of cancer.
  • Some functional cysts resolve; not every solid, complex or persistent mass behaves the same way.
  • Ultrasound, pregnancy status and individual risks guide tests, monitoring or surgery.
  • Sudden severe pelvic pain, collapse or signs of internal bleeding require emergency care.
  • Pregnancy needs an individualized plan, not a fixed cancer percentage or automatic treatment delay.

Frequently asked questions

When does an adnexal mass need treatment?

Treatment depends on symptoms, growth, scan features, life stage and the suspected cause. A reassuring simple cyst may be observed. Persistent, growing, complex or suspicious findings need further review, and acute complications require urgent care; not every solid mass automatically needs surgery.

What symptoms can it cause?

Some cause none. Pelvic pain, period changes, pain during sex, bloating, urinary pressure or frequency, constipation and digestive symptoms are possible. Persistent changes should be checked, while sudden severe pain, fainting or collapse needs emergency assessment.

How is it diagnosed?

History and examination are followed by ultrasound in most cases, with pregnancy testing and other tests as appropriate. MRI or specialist imaging can clarify uncertain findings. Neither symptoms nor a single blood marker can establish every diagnosis.

What happens if the mass is small and painless?

A simple, reassuring cyst may need no immediate treatment; follow-up depends on its appearance and your circumstances. Ask whether a repeat scan is needed and when. Do not assume small size makes every mass harmless or that no pain means follow-up can be skipped.

Does a solid or complex mass mean cancer?

No. Benign lesions may contain solid tissue or complex material, but those features need proper assessment. Cancer risk depends on the whole picture, and suspicious findings may require specialist referral or tissue examination.

What if I am pregnant?

Tell the team so pregnancy location, scan findings and any blood tests are interpreted appropriately. Many reassuring cysts can be monitored, but symptoms or concerning features may need intervention. Severe pain or faintness must not wait for routine pregnancy follow-up.

Can BeMama tell whether my mass is benign?

No. It can help organize symptoms and appointment dates, but cannot interpret a scan, exclude ectopic pregnancy or cancer, or decide whether surgery is needed. Seek clinical assessment and follow the agreed plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
